vignette:
He sits at his desk in the spare bedroom that doubles as his home office, the glow of three monitors washing over his face at 3:17 a.m. The log files for his client’s network scroll past, line after line of encrypted traffic, and his eyes catch the smallest irregularity—a packet header two bytes off, a timestamp out of sequence. He flags it, writes a note for the morning team, and only then does he realize his hands are trembling. He hasn’t slept more than two hours a night since last Tuesday, a pattern he recognizes but cannot break.

That pattern began forty-seven years ago, though he did not see it then.

His son, Tam, was four. A fever that wouldn’t break, then the rash, then the word *meningitis* spoken in a hushed tone by a young doctor who could not have been older than thirty. He remembers the hospital corridor, the strip of yellow paint along the wall, the smell of antiseptic so thick it coated the back of his throat. He remembers his wife, Lien, gripping his arm so tightly that her nails left half-moons in his skin. He remembers the machine that beeped in sync with Tam’s heart, and how he counted every single beat as if his own life depended on it.

Tam survived. The antibiotics worked, the fever dropped, and within two weeks he was home, drawing crayon pictures of dogs with lopsided ears. The doctors called it a full recovery. For Lien, the nightmare ended. For him, it simply changed shape.

He started checking on Tam at night—three, four, five times. He would stand over his son’s bed and wait for the rising and falling of the chest. He began not leaving the house without a fully stocked emergency kit. He cancelled family outings because the weather might turn, because the car might break down, because something unnameable might happen. Lien said he was smothering the boy. He said she didn’t understand.

He became a cybersecurity analyst because it was the only field in which standing watch, scanning for threats, and refusing to let your guard down were considered virtues. He rose early, stayed late, imagined every possible breach and built a wall against it. His employers praised his vigilance. His colleagues called him obsessive, but they said it with respect.

When Lien died of a stroke twelve years ago, the world did not end—it just went quiet. He was alone with his watch. Tam grew up, moved to another city, became an architect, married, had children. And still, each month, his father calls to ask about their health, their blood pressure, the last time they had a checkup. The grandchildren know him as the grandfather who sends vitamin packets and links to articles about lead in tap water. They do not know that when Tam doesn’t answer the phone by the second ring, he replays the memory of that yellow hospital wall, the beeping, the feeling of his own heart stopping.

Now, at seventy-five, he works only as a part-time consultant, but the hours he keeps are those of a man who has never learned to rest. The PCL-5 score of 74 means something to the clinicians at the VA clinic he finally visited last month, but he does not think in numbers. He thinks in the tightness behind his eyes when he replays the inhaler that ran out at a sleepover when Tam was eleven, the allergic reaction to a bee sting at sixteen, the scripted “There’s nothing to worry about” from a doctor during Tam’s fiftieth birthday party, which he heard as a lie.

Every time a new system log registers a false alarm, he feels a flicker of relief—then anger at himself for feeling relief, because that means the real alarm might come while he is distracted. He keeps an old photograph of Tam at age four on his desk, tucked under the monitor. He does not look at it often. He does not need to. The image is burned into the back of his eyelids, waiting for him every time he closes them.
